title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 99–100

units.title: Unit 99 — Informal emails and messages
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 204–205 (PDF pages 205–206).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Informal email and messaging language, greetings, closings and conversational phrases
learningObjectives: Open and close informal emails with greetings and sign-offs suited to friends and relatives.
Use friendly ways to thank someone, arrange plans, and convey regards or love.
Apply get or be in touch, let someone know, fancy + -ing, get together and join someone accurately.
Express elapsed time and future dates using ages since and in a number of weeks’ time.
Distinguish actually or in fact from currently or at the moment.
Recognise expressions that signal a positive response, a topic change or the end of a conversation.

items.example: Hi, Maya! It was great to hear from you.
items.note: A friendly informal greeting before a person's name; Hi Maya is a natural email opening.

items.example: Hello, Jack! I hope you're doing well.
items.note: A greeting suitable for friendly emails; can be slightly less casual than Hi.

items.pt: caro; querida (vocativo em carta ou e-mail)
items.example: Dear Emma, thank you for your lovely note.
items.note: Also possible in informal emails to people you know; the tone depends on the relationship.

items.example: Just a quick message to check that you arrived safely.
items.note: A conversational way to introduce a short email or message.

items.example: I want to thank you for your help with the move.
items.note: Use thank + person + for + noun or -ing, for example thank her for coming.

items.example: The meal was absolutely delicious.
items.note: Absolutely intensifies strong evaluative adjectives such as delicious.

items.example: Your advice was helpful, as always.
items.note: Means as on previous occasions.

items.pt: ser divertido; ser uma pessoa engraçada
items.example: Your cousin is a laugh; he always makes us smile.
items.note: Informal British English: a person who is funny and enjoyable to spend time with.

items.pt: estar esperando; ter a esperança de fazer algo
items.example: We're hoping to visit you next month.
items.note: Be hoping to + infinitive indicates a plan or intention that is not yet certain.

items.example: We're trying to get tickets for the concert.
items.note: Get tickets for + event means obtain admission tickets.

items.example: I'll be in touch when I know the dates.
items.note: Means make contact in the future or stay in communication; often followed by with + person.

items.example: I'll get in touch after my exam.
items.note: Often used with with + person, e.g. get in touch with her.

items.pt: estar a fim de fazer algo
items.example: Do you fancy going to the cinema on Friday?
items.note: Informal British English; fancy + -ing means want to do something, not fancy to do.

items.pt: estar a fim de assistir a algo
items.example: Is there a film you fancy seeing this weekend?
items.note: A specific use of fancy + -ing with films or shows.

items.example: Please give my regards to your parents.
items.note: Ask someone to pass on your greetings; relatively polite but also suitable for friendly messages.

items.example: Send my regards to Daniel when you see him.
items.note: An alternative to give my regards to someone.

items.pt: mande meu carinho; mande um abraço carinhoso para alguém
items.example: Give my love to your grandmother.
items.note: More affectionate than regards; for family and very close friends.

items.example: Send my love to the children.
items.note: An affectionate alternative to give my love to.

items.example: Once again, thanks for inviting me.
items.note: Used to repeat a sentiment or thank someone another time.

items.example: Love, Hannah.
items.note: An informal sign-off for someone close to you; the word itself is the audio target, not an entire signature.

items.example: Lots of love, Mum.
items.note: An affectionate informal sign-off, often used with family and close friends.

items.pt: tudo de bom; votos de felicidades
items.example: Best wishes, Olivia.
items.note: A friendly closing, less intimate than Love.

items.example: All the best, Ben.
items.note: A warm and flexible closing for messages to friends.

items.pt: faz muito tempo; faz uma eternidade
items.example: It's been ages since we last spoke.
items.note: Informal: a long time has passed; commonly followed by since + past event.

items.example: It's ages since I saw my school friends.
items.note: Since connects the elapsed period with a past action or event.

items.example: I've lived here since I started university.
items.note: Refers to a starting time or event in the past; often used with the present perfect.

items.example: Please let me know when you arrive.
items.note: Let + person + know; the person goes before know, e.g. let us know.

items.example: The new course starts in two weeks' time.
items.note: Means two weeks from now; the apostrophe follows weeks, a plural word.

items.example: I'll send you the photos in a week's time.
items.note: Singular possessive week's; contrast with plural two weeks' time.

items.example: I thought it was Friday, but actually it's Thursday.
items.note: Means in fact, or introduces more exact or unexpected information; not a translation of currently.

items.example: The house looks small; in fact, it has five bedrooms.
items.note: Can introduce a correction or something surprising; a synonym of actually in these contexts.

items.example: The flat is currently available to rent.
items.note: Means at the moment, not the same as actually.

items.example: He's working from home at the moment.
items.note: Refers to the present period; contrast with actually or in fact.

items.example: A picnic by the lake? Sounds great!
items.note: An informal enthusiastic response to a suggestion.

items.example: When exactly are you arriving?
items.note: Asks for a precise date or time.

items.example: Let's get together for coffee next week.
items.note: Meet socially; different from get in touch, which may be by phone or message.

items.pt: sair para comer fora; sair para uma refeição
items.example: We might go out for a meal after the film.
items.note: Go to a restaurant or another place to eat socially.

items.example: Would you like to join us for lunch?
items.note: Join + people: come with or become part of the group; no preposition after join here.

items.example: Could Sophie join you for dinner?
items.note: You join someone, not join with someone, in this sense.

items.example: I'll book a restaurant for Saturday evening.
items.note: Informal shorthand for booking a table at a restaurant; book a table is more explicit.

items.example: Anyway, I'd better finish this report.
items.note: Discourse marker used to move on, return to a topic, or end a conversation.

items.example: I'd better get back to work now.
items.note: Informal shortened wording with had better; means return to working.

items.example: See you soon! I hope we can meet on Tuesday.
items.note: Friendly closing when you expect to see someone again soon.

items.example: I hope things are going well with you.
items.note: A warm expression about how someone's life is progressing.

units.title: Unit 100 — Abbreviations
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 206–207 (PDF pages 207–208).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Initialisms, acronyms, written abbreviations, Latin abbreviations and shortened everyday words
learningObjectives: Identify common initial-letter abbreviations and give the expansions supplied by the book.
Distinguish abbreviations spoken letter by letter, words pronounced as words, and forms written short but read in full.
Use stand for to ask what a shortened form means.
Recognise etc., e.g. and i.e. and distinguish their functions.
Use everyday shortened words naturally in informal communication and recognise their longer equivalents.
Understand common written or digital abbreviations such as PTO, RSVP, asap, IMO, DOB and PS.

items.example: An abbreviation makes a word or phrase shorter.
items.note: Some are spoken as letter names, others as words, and some are only shorter in writing.

items.example: The EU includes several different countries.
items.note: European Union; say the names of the letters E and U.

items.example: The UN organised a meeting about the crisis.
items.note: United Nations; pronounce U and N separately.

items.example: The PM made a statement this morning.
items.note: Prime Minister in the book's British political example; spoken P M. Not the time abbreviation p.m.

items.example: She wrote to her local MP about the problem.
items.note: Member of Parliament; spoken M P, not Minister of Parliament.

items.example: I heard the news on the BBC.
items.note: British Broadcasting Corporation; say the individual letters B B C.

items.example: You need to show ID to collect the parcel.
items.note: Short for identification; spoken I D.

items.pt: documento de identidade; cartão de identificação
items.example: Please bring your ID card to the appointment.
items.note: An identification card; pronounce I D as two letter names.

items.example: I use a PC for most of my work.
items.note: Personal computer; spoken P C.

items.example: Please attach your CV to the application.
items.note: Curriculum vitae, a record of education and work experience; spoken C V.

items.example: I called my ISP because the connection stopped working.
items.note: Internet Service Provider; spoken I S P, not Internet Service Player.

items.example: AIDS is an example of an abbreviation spoken as a word.
items.note: Pronounced as one word, unlike abbreviations read as separate letters.

items.pt: número de identificação pessoal; senha numérica
items.example: Never tell anyone your bank card PIN.
items.note: Personal identification number; spoken as the single word pin, rather than separate letters.

items.example: What does ISP stand for?
items.note: Use what does + abbreviation + stand for? to ask for its full form.

items.section: B · Written forms spoken in full
items.example: Mr Parker called while you were away.
items.note: Written as Mr but pronounced mister.

items.section: B · Written forms spoken in full
items.example: Mrs Brown teaches French at our school.
items.note: Written as Mrs but pronounced missiz; traditionally a title for a married woman.

items.section: B · Written forms spoken in full
items.example: Dr Patel can see you on Monday.
items.note: Written as Dr but pronounced doctor; commonly used for physicians or people with doctorates.

items.section: B · Written forms spoken in full
items.example: The wedding is at St Mary's Church.
items.note: Before a saint's name, St is pronounced Saint. Distinct from St meaning Street.

items.section: B · Written forms spoken in full
items.example: Her office is on King St.
items.note: In a street name or address, St is pronounced Street, not Saint.

items.example: Bring a notebook, a pen, a ruler, etc.
items.note: From Latin et cetera; means and so on and is usually spoken et cetera.

items.example: Choose a warm drink, e.g. tea or coffee.
items.note: From Latin exempli gratia; means for example; pronounced as letter names E G.

items.example: We need a bilingual person, i.e. someone who speaks two languages.
items.note: From Latin id est; means that is or in other words, not for example.

items.example: My phone was on the kitchen table.
items.note: A shortened form of telephone; very common in speech.

items.example: Maths was my favourite subject at school.
items.note: British English shortening of mathematics; American English often uses math.

items.example: The teacher wrote a new word on the board.
items.note: Short for whiteboard, smartboard or blackboard in a classroom context.

items.example: I packed my case the night before we left.
items.note: Informal shortened form of suitcase; case has other meanings in other contexts.

items.example: We saw an ad for the job online.
items.note: Short for advertisement; informal, especially common in writing and speech.

items.example: She answered an advert in the local paper.
items.note: British English shortening of advertisement, also called an ad.

items.example: I go to the gym twice a week.
items.note: Shortened form of gymnasium; the long form can sound formal or old-fashioned.

items.example: He rides his bike to work.
items.note: Short for bicycle; bike can also mean motorcycle in some contexts.

items.example: There's a documentary on TV tonight.
items.note: An initial-letter shortened form of television; say T V.

items.example: We watched the match on the telly.
items.note: Very informal British English for television.

items.example: Dad reads the paper before breakfast.
items.note: In this context, a shortening of newspaper; paper has other senses.

items.example: Put the milk back in the fridge.
items.note: Short for refrigerator.

items.example: I have an exam on Thursday.
items.note: Short for examination.

items.example: Our plane landed twenty minutes late.
items.note: Short for aeroplane in British English; airplane in American English.

items.example: Can you send me a photo of your dog?
items.note: Short for photograph.

items.example: He stayed home because he had the flu.
items.note: Short for influenza; not the same as an ordinary cold.

items.example: The students carried out the experiment in the lab.
items.note: Short for laboratory.

items.example: A sales rep visited our office yesterday.
items.note: Short for sales representative; a salesperson is a related term.

items.example: We took our cat to the vet.
items.note: Common short form of veterinary surgeon.

items.pt: vire a página; veja o verso
items.example: PTO appears at the bottom of this page.
items.note: Please turn over; printed on a page to indicate that there is more on the reverse side.

items.example: The invitation asks guests to RSVP by Friday.
items.note: French Répondez s'il vous plaît, meaning please reply; common on invitations.

items.pt: o quanto antes; assim que possível
items.example: Please send me the file asap.
items.note: As soon as possible; common in messages and emails.

items.example: IMO, the second option looks better.
items.note: In my opinion; informal online and messaging abbreviation.

items.example: Enter your DOB on the form.
items.note: Date of birth; often seen on forms.

items.example: PS: I left your book on the desk.
items.note: Postscript; extra information added after the signature at the end of a letter.
